question.prompt:
The plane is tiled by congruent squares and congruent pentagons as indicated. The percent of the plane that is enclosed by the pentagons is closest to

[Figure 1](figures/2001_AMC_10_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

solutions.explanation:
A repeating block makes the area comparison easier: we can subtract the square tiles from the whole block without calculating each pentagon separately.

[Figure 1](figures/2001_AMC_10_Q18_question_fig1.svg)

First assume that the central horizontal and vertical strips have the same width as a square tile's side. This is the intended metric interpretation of the drawing, rather than a marked equality. Let that common length be \(s>0\). The upper-left repeating block then has side \(3s\), with four square tiles at its corners and four pentagons filling the remainder. Its area is \(9s^2\), and its square tiles occupy \(4s^2\). Thus the pentagon percentage is
\[
\frac{9s^2-4s^2}{9s^2}\times100\%
=\frac59\times100\%
\approx55.56\%.
\]
Copies of this block fill the plane without overlapping interiors, so the same percentage applies to the plane. Under this assumption, the closest choice is \(56\), choice D.

We must distinguish an assumption that guarantees D from an assumption required for D. To examine the unmarked width, choose the square side as one unit and let the central strip width be \(w>0\). Construct a block of side \(2+w\), placing a unit square at each corner. Join each square's inward-facing corner to the center of the block. The remaining region is partitioned into four pentagons. Each consists of a \(1\)-by-\(w\) rectangle and a triangle with base \(w\) and height \(w/2\). Quarter-turns about the center carry these pentagons onto one another, so they are congruent for every positive \(w\).

Repeating the block horizontally and vertically fills the plane: neighboring blocks have matching boundary segments, and each block is completely partitioned into its four squares and four pentagons. Thus there are no gaps or overlapping interiors. The pentagon percentage is
\[
P(w)=\left(1-\frac{4}{(2+w)^2}\right)100\%.
\]
The denominator is positive because \(w>0\).

When \(w=1\), this gives the exact fraction \(5/9\). But when \(w=1.01\), it gives approximately \(55.85\%\), still closest to D even though the strip width differs from the square side. Equal widths are therefore sufficient, but not necessary, for D to be closest.

On the other hand, when \(w=0.9\), the same construction gives
\[
P(0.9)=\left(1-\frac{400}{841}\right)100\%
=\frac{441}{841}\times100\%
\approx52.44\%,
\]
whose closest choice is B, \(52\). Consequently, congruence and the indicated arrangement alone do not determine a unique closest choice when the widths are unspecified. The conditional equal-width result is \(5/9\), approximately \(55.56\%\), choice D.
solutions.title: A repeating block and the width qualification
